<reason>Both sides executed at a high level with clean format compliance and plausible background knowledge. Side A built the stronger path to victory: the "prediction contradiction" pressure (Q1) forced Side B onto the back foot, and while B's hypothesis-versus-verdict distinction was a genuinely good answer, it never fully squared with the motion's own "clear pandemic potential" threshold—if the danger is clear enough to justify building it, it is clear enough to ban. Side A also landed the sharper weighing: a demonstrated failure mode (lab escapes at top facilities) with civilizational downside versus a speculative, replaceable preparation benefit, crystallized memorably as "a bit slower" versus "millions of deaths." Side B's best live routes—the nature-publishes-the-roadmap point and the overbreadth/chilling-effect argument—were answered respectably (published roadmaps arm adversaries too; existing dual-use review already draws such lines) but not fully reversed, and B's overbreadth framing slightly mismatches the motion as written. Side A's clipped opening (losing the tail of the enforceability argument) and the unresolved bird-flu surveillance knowledge point are real costs, keeping this competitive rather than decisive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was Side A's Q1 (if your researchers can predict pandemic potential to justify the experiment, why can't a regulator predict it to ban it?) followed by Side B's B4.1 hypothesis-versus-verdict answer and Side A's closing reassertion. B's answer was the best defensive move of the debate, but A's closing framing—"if it isn't clear, no one is being prepared, they are rolling dice with a civilization-scale hazard"—left the contradiction as the controlling clash and gave the cleanest reason to vote for the ban.</best_rebuttal>
